Title: Dynamic small object feature enhancement and detection for remote sensing images
Text:
Dynamic small object feature 
enhancement and detection for 
remote sensing images
Shouluan Wu1, Hui Yang1, Liefa Liao1,2, Chao Song1, Qiuming Liu1, Jianglong Fu3 & 
Tan Li4
Remote sensing images are extensively utilized for Earth observation; however, they often encounter 
challenges such as extremely small objects, cluttered backgrounds, and constraints related to edge 
computing. Current studies frequently face difficulties in achieving an optimal balance between 
recognition accuracy and efficiency to satisfy the requirements of various embedded devices. We 
propose DFE-DETR, a lightweight dynamic feature-enhanced detector that refines RT-DETR for 
remote-sensing scenes. The model relies on three core modules: the Sparse Attention Enhancement 
Module (SAEM) that prunes irrelevant tokens via Top-k scoring to cut compute, the Multi-scale 
Convolutional Attention Enhancement Module (MSCAEM) that employs multi-branch depth-wise 
strip convolutions to sharpen slender targets, and the Deformable Large Kernel Convolution Module 
(DLKCM) that uses adaptive sampling to locate irregular objects. Experiments demonstrate that this 
framework achieves a significant performance breakthrough on the VisDrone2019 dataset with only 
23.6 M parameters, reaching 47.34% mAP@0.5 and 65.8 FPS. On the SIMD dataset, it attains 82.79% 
mAP@0.5 and 74.6 FPS. Meanwhile, on the RSOD and NWPU VHR-10 datasets, it achieves mAP@0.5 
scores of 96.58% and 93.28%, respectively. Ablation experiments validate the synergistic effects 
of the modules, and visualization heatmaps indicate that the proposed model provides the most 
comprehensive target perception, accurately delineating target contours. In comparative experiments, 
the model outperformed mainstream YOLO series and specialized UAV detection models, offering a 
new high-precision real-time detection solution for embedded scenarios such as disaster response and 
traffic monitoring.
Keywords  Remote sensing object detection, UAV, Deformable conv, DETR
 In recent years, the rapid advancement of remote sensing technology has propelled small target recognition 
in aerial imagery to the forefront of computer vision research1,2. Leveraging its extensive coverage advantages, 
aerial remote sensing imagery has been widely utilized in critical scenarios such as disaster emergency 
response4, urban traffic monitoring5, and agricultural resource surveys6. However, constrained by sensor 
resolution and the high-altitude imaging characteristics, targets often exhibit features such as small size, low 
contrast, and insufficient information density7. Simultaneously, the nonlinear scale–height relationship of UAV 
platforms—where slight changes in flight altitude can cause significant fluctuations in target scale—along with 
motion blur induced by high-speed movement and complex scene interference, makes foreground/background 
differentiation exceptionally challenging, imposing higher demands for high-precision real-time detection. 
Although existing methods demonstrate acceptable localization accuracy, they suffer from high computational 
complexity and poor real-time performance, urgently requiring lightweight designs and multi-scale feature 
fusion to enhance system robustness. Object detection technology has evolved from manual feature engineering 
to deep learning methods. Two-stage detectors (e.g., Faster R-CNN8 achieve high-precision localization through 
a region proposal network and a refined classification cascade, while single-stage detectors (e.g., RetinaNet, 
YOLO series9,10 balance real-time performance with end-to-end multi-scale feature pyramids and have been 
widely applied in industrial scenarios involving tiny objects. Ahmed Gomaa’s team further improved YOLOv8 
with low-rank decomposition, significantly reducing manual annotation through hierarchical clustering11.

In 2020, Facebook AI Research introduced the Detection Transformer (DETR), which was the first model 
to achieve end-to-end object detection using a pure Transformer architecture. This innovation overcame the 
limitations of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in terms of receptive fields by employing a self-attention 
mechanism, thereby demonstrating exceptional performance in complex scene association reasoning12. 
However, its high computational cost and the challenges associated with post-processing still impede practical 
deployment. To address these issues, RT-DETR surpasses both the accuracy and speed of the YOLO series at 
the same scale, thanks to its non-maximum suppression (NMS)-free design13. In the context of remote sensing 
imagery, the relationship between platform altitude and target scale is nonlinear: a mere change of tens of 
meters in flight altitude can lead to a multiplicative scaling of the same target within the image. Furthermore, 
motion blur caused by high-speed movement and interference from complex backgrounds intensify the need 
for cross-scale feature consistency and real-time performance. Therefore, it is essential to introduce a lightweight 
dynamic enhancement mechanism tailored for UAV scenarios within the DETR/RT-DETR framework to 
improve the robustness of small target detection. Inspired by the Transformer, Xue et al. proposed a cross-
UAV framework that utilizes regional semantic association modeling and multi-head sparse self-attention. By 
adaptively capturing invariant target information from heterogeneous images and integrating a multi-view 
correction strategy, this framework effectively fuses complementary information across UAVs, significantly 
reducing background interference and addressing illumination variations14. The core innovations of RT-DETR 
include two key aspects: first, a hybrid encoder architecture for multimodal feature fusion is designed, achieving 
multiscale semantic representation through cross-level feature interaction; second, a novel Intersection over 
Union (IoU)-based dynamic query initialization mechanism is introduced, which directly filters effective object 
queries from the encoder output using a spatial location-sensitive IoU matching strategy, thereby eliminating 
the redundant region proposal steps typical of traditional two-stage methods. Compared to the original DETR 
architecture, RT-DETR completely eliminates post-processing steps such as NMS.
By comprehensively capturing target characteristics, researchers have significantly improved the processing 
efficiency and accuracy of real-time object detection systems through the introduction of multi-scale feature 
fusion and attention mechanisms, enabling the algorithm to achieve effective recognition in complex scenarios. 
The research team proposed a real-time aerial vehicle tracking framework that integrates morphological 
detection and motion feature analysis. This framework employs an adaptive method for multi-scale vehicle 
initial detection and utilizes the KLT tracker along with K-means clustering to mitigate background interference, 
thereby achieving collaborative optimization of detection and tracking15. In response to the increasing complexity 
of networks and the growing number of computational parameters, Shen et al. developed a lightweight deep 
convolutional network and a hybrid attention fine-grained feature recognition framework. They reduced the 
computational load by implementing a lightweight single-scale detection algorithm and designed a hybrid 
attention pruning mechanism to enhance fine-grained classification capabilities, achieving multi-stage 
collaborative optimization of localization and recognition16,17. Researchers are currently focusing on model 
lightweighting while incorporating a lightweight multi-scale feature extraction network. The semantic feature 
enhancement module integrates contextual information with residual attention, enabling high-precision target 
recognition18. Xue et al. proposed a UAV vision-language tracking framework based on Dynamic Sparse Learning 
and Multi-Level Language Perception which generates multimodal prompts through dynamic sparse attention 
and combines an efficient Transformer backbone network to facilitate sparse interaction between language and 
visual features, significantly enhancing the robustness of target representation19. Xue et al.20 proposed a three-
stage query-guided re-detection tracker based on Siamese neural networks. This approach maintains target 
appearance features through a dynamic query update (QU) branch, utilizes a cross-fusion layer (CFL) to search 
for semantic associations between features and updated queries, thereby enhancing the distinction of occluded 
targets. Additionally, it employs Kalman filter trajectory prediction (TP) to stabilize tracking trajectories 
during complete occlusion, which significantly improves the tracking robustness of occluded targets in UAV 
scenarios. Furthermore, researchers have proposed a UAV target tracking method based on global proxies to 
address challenges such as background interference in target recognition21. This method dynamically aggregates 
features from both target and background regions through a target-distractor perception module, models 
global dependencies using a self-attention mechanism, and guides local feature generation to enhance target 
distinctiveness, which significantly improves tracking capabilities in complex backgrounds.
Currently, the deployment of high-performance real-time detection systems is constrained by the 
computational resources of aviation platforms, presenting significant technical challenges. Hardware constraints 
make it difficult to achieve an optimal balance between detection accuracy and computational efficiency on 
embedded platforms. These conflicting relationships necessitate that algorithm design establish a dynamic balance 
mechanism among model lightweighting, feature representation completeness, and hardware adaptability. To 
address these challenges, this paper proposes a small object detection scheme for UAV perspectives called DFE-
DETR, which is based on an improved RT-DETR architecture. This approach facilitates the effective integration 
and extraction of features and enhances the model’s capability to recognize multi-angle targets, thereby 
significantly improving detection performance. The main contributions of this paper are as follows:
•	 We have developed a Dynamic Sparse Attention Enhancement Module (SAEM) specifically designed to ac­
curately capture complex features and relevant regions in image data, thereby significantly enhancing model 
performance in object detection tasks.
•	 We have designed a Multi-Scale Convolutional Attention Enhancement Module (MSCAEM) to extract de­
tailed feature information. This module aggregates local features through deep convolution and captures in­
formation at various scales using multi-branch deep strip convolution.

Relate works
Generic vs. UAV detectors
Early architectures fall into two camps: two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN, Cascade R-CNN22 for precision, and 
single-stage ones (SSD23, YOLO family24,25 for speed. In UAV imagery, however, the non-linear scale–altitude 
relationship and extreme small-target sparsity quickly expose the limits of fixed-grid YOLO heads and naïve 
FPN/PANet fusion26–28. Consequently, recent UAV-oriented variants compress and re-scale the YOLO backbone: 
YOLO-HR adds lightweight hybrid ECA + CA attention29, Yu et al. embed weighted BiFPN for SAR ships30, 
RCA31 and MLCA32 insert channel- or mixed-local attention to suppress high-altitude clutter. UAV-YOLO33, 
Drone-YOLO34, FFCA-YOLO7 and YOLO-MIF35 further trim parameters and refine multi-scale heads, yet al.l 
keep the underlying 3 × 3 convolutional inductive bias, leaving irregular, elongated targets under-represented.
Limitations analysis of current solutions
Despite the foundational role of traditional computer vision paradigms in the development of UAV detection, 
the unique imaging conditions of UAV platforms—characterized by high-altitude perspectives, dynamic 
lighting variations, and complex terrains—introduce multidimensional challenges. These challenges encompass 
geometric distortions arising from multi-angle observations, edge blurring due to background clutter, variable 
target scale and orientation distributions, and declining recall rates for small targets under low-resolution 
conditions36. To mitigate these issues, researchers have implemented targeted optimizations through task-
specific scenario subdivisions. Notably, the nonlinear relationship between target height and size in UAV 
imagery necessitates transcending traditional single-scale detection frameworks. Cutting-edge methods now 
utilize pyramid multi-scale feature fusion architectures (e.g., hybrid FPN-BiFPN modules) and dynamic scale 
adaptation mechanisms (including adaptive anchor box generation and multi-resolution feature interaction), 
which have significantly enhanced small object detection performance while preserving real-time capabilities37. 
The research team aimed to extract small feature targets while eliminating background interference, proposing 
an aerial small object tracker based on the Siamese network architecture. They innovatively integrated a Wavelet 
Pooling Layer (WPL) that extracts both high-frequency and low-frequency sub-band features, retaining 
discriminative information through wavelet domain decomposition. Additionally, they combined this with a 
Graph Enhancement Module (GEM), which leverages graph neural networks to emphasize target responses. 
This collaborative approach effectively addresses the challenges associated with small object feature loss and 
background interference38. Current research has proposed multi-dimensional technical solutions, such as 
incorporating dilated or deformable convolutional kernels at the feature extraction level to improve scale 
adaptability. However, the physical characteristics of high-altitude UAV operations—marked by diverse target 
scales and miniature dimensions—continue to pose challenges. Alternatively, real-time detection and tracking 
of UAVs can be achieved by employing morphological and feature clustering methods. By utilizing K-means 
clustering, moving feature points are effectively separated to mitigate background interference. Furthermore, the 
challenges of occlusion and scale variation are addressed through the integration of a tracker with a trajectory 
connection mechanism39. To address these, researchers have introduced cascade detection architectures, multi-
scale feature fusion networks, lightweight attention mechanisms, and HRDNet optimizations for dense target 
scenarios40–42. Through the synergistic optimization of scale-adaptive feature engineering and lightweight 
network design, these methods substantially enhance small target detection capabilities in UAV contexts 
while maintaining real-time performance. Sabina Umirzakova et al. proposed the RASST lightweight rotation-
aware semi-supervised Transformer framework, which integrates a rotation-aware Vision Transformer (ViT) 
architecture with an adaptive rotation convolution module. This framework achieves precise alignment of target 
orientations through dynamically adjusted rotating convolution kernels and incorporates a pseudo-label guided 
learning (PGL) approach. Furthermore, it combines rotation-aware adaptive weighting (RAW) and global 
consistency (GC) loss to optimize annotated data, significantly enhancing the detection robustness of multi-
angle targets in aerial images while reducing the number of parameters43.
Recent efforts have focused on mitigating the adverse effects of Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) on small 
target detection, particularly in the context of remote sensing. Achieving intelligent interpretation of high-
quality images remains a core challenge in this field. The RT-DETR model offers an efficient solution for multi-
scale detection through its hybrid encoder architecture and unordered set prediction paradigm44. Mainstream 
Transformer-based object detectors, such as DINO and Focus-DETR, demonstrate high accuracy in general 
scenarios. However, their excessive computational load and deficiencies in real-time performance severely 
hinder deployment on UAV edge devices. Taking DINO as an example, its multi-layer Transformer encoder 
and cross-scale fusion design cause the FLOPs per frame to skyrocket to 273.7G. Meanwhile, Focus-DETR, 
despite optimizations through local attention, still requires 171.5G FLOPs, significantly exceeding the hardware 
limitations of onboard systems. The rationale for selecting RT-DETR as a baseline model stems from this issue. 
It employs a collaborative architecture that combines a CNN backbone with a lightweight Transformer encoder, 
significantly reducing GFLOPs and achieving real-time performance recognition capabilities. Moreover, it 
circumvents the post-processing delay associated with NMS through a single-pass decoding design. This design 
greatly optimizes computational efficiency while ensuring accuracy, aligning precisely with the core demand for a 
“speed-accuracy balance” in UAV missions and providing an engineering-level solution for resource-constrained 
scenarios. This architecture effectively decouples intra-scale feature interaction from cross-level multi-scale

an unordered set prediction problem, RT-DETR employs a sparse query mechanism to directly generate object 
candidate boxes, thus avoiding the computational overhead associated with NMS in YOLO detectors45. Within 
the unordered set prediction framework, the model requires only feature classification score ranking for final 
predictions, thereby eliminating delays caused by dense candidate box generation and iterative NMS processes 
inherent in conventional methods. Despite RT-DETR’s superiority over existing real-time detectors and similarly 
scaled end-to-end frameworks in terms of speed and accuracy, it encounters performance bottlenecks in small 
object detection—specifically in localization precision and recall rates—when compared to high-performance 
real-time detectors. This limitation primarily arises from deficiencies in feature extraction, notably insufficient 
dense sampling and inadequate multi-scale representation capabilities. To address these gaps, we propose an 
efficient framework, Dynamic Feature Enhancement DETR (DFE-DETR), aimed at improving remote sensing 
image analysis. Departing from these incremental YOLO derivatives, DFE-DETR retains RT-DETR’s end-to-
end Transformer backbone but introduces the Deformable Large-Kernel Convolution Module (DLKCM), a 
biomimetic receptive-field expansion inspired by primate visual cortex neurons. Unlike previous small-kernel 
or static dilated designs, DLKCM learns irregular sampling offsets on-the-fly, enabling the network to “stretch” 
its receptive field along arbitrary target axes while keeping computation linear in the number of sampled points. 
Coupled with the Sparse Attention Enhancement (SAEM) and Multi-Scale Convolutional Attention (MSCAEM) 
modules, DFE-DETR thus uniquely addresses UAV-specific scale variance and anisotropic target shapes without 
the parameter explosion seen in recent YOLO variants.
Method
DFE-DETR architecture
To address the challenges of object detection in complex remote sensing scenarios, this study proposes a dynamic 
multi-scale feature enhancement detection framework (DFE-DETR) based on the RT-DETR architecture. The 
overall structure of the model is illustrated in Fig. 1. First, ResNet-18 is utilized as the backbone network to 
extract global image features, resulting in high-semantic feature S5, mid-semantic feature S4, and low-semantic 
feature S3. High-semantic features contain rich information. These features are connected with the Sparse 
Attention Enhancement Module (SAEM), which enables the attention mechanism to concentrate on target 
features and extract detailed information. Additionally, a dynamic sparse attention module is employed to 
facilitate adaptive sparse weight allocation, which is closely integrated with the AIFI (Attention-based Intra-scale 
Feature Interaction) module to achieve adaptive feature fusion. This enhancement improves the representation 
of common features among similar target elements (such as buildings and vehicles) in remote sensing images, 
while also suppressing background noise interference. Subsequently, a multi-scale convolutional feature 
interaction network was constructed in the CCFM (Cross-Scale Feature Fusion Module), utilizing a multi-scale 
convolutional attention module. This module employs multiple sets of multi-scale convolutional kernels to 
extract spatial features across various granularities. This approach achieves dynamic feature complementarity and 
spatial attention excitation through an element-wise multiplication mechanism. Simultaneously, a deformable 
convolutional layer is introduced to adaptively adjust the sampling grid, effectively addressing the diversity in 
target scale, pose, and imaging modalities. These modules collaborate through various operations, including 
Fusion, Upsampling, 1 × 1 convolutional channel transformation, and RepC3, to generate queries that are rich 
in semantic information. The Decoder on the right processes this query in conjunction with encoder features, 
reconstructing and refining the features through the Decoder and Head module. Finally, a detection head with 
shared weights is employed for the joint regression prediction of target categories and bounding box parameters, 
striking a balance between computational efficiency and representational accuracy. In the following sections, I 
will provide a detailed description of each component of the DFE-DETR architecture.

SAEM
Our designed dynamic sparse attention augmentation module represents an efficient enhancement of the 
traditional Transformer self-attention mechanism. The core concept of this module is to dynamically filter key 
regions in the input sequence, thereby reducing computational complexity while maintaining the perception 
of global information. Specifically, the module first generates importance scores for each position based on 
input features, subsequently selecting the most relevant local regions and global key points through a Top-k 
strategy. Dense attention calculations are then performed exclusively on the sparsely selected regions. This 
mechanism reduces the O(N²) complexity of traditional self-attention mechanisms to O(kN) (where k ≪ N). 
The dynamic sparse mechanism significantly minimizes redundant computations and adapts to the features of 
varying samples. In remote sensing image tasks, such as high-resolution image detection, this module strikes 
a balance between efficiency and accuracy, offering a lightweight solution for complex perception tasks in 
resource-sensitive scenarios.

MSCAEM
After passing through the SAEM and AIFI modules, the features undergo adaptive feature fusion. In response 
to the unique shapes of various targets in drone images, we have designed a multi-scale convolutional attention 
enhancement module to extract detailed feature information more effectively. This module aggregates local 
features through depthwise convolution and captures information at different scales using multi-branch 
depthwise strip convolution, as illustrated in Fig.  3. Building on this, a 1 × 1 convolution establishes inter-
channel relationships, and its output serves as attention weights to adaptively adjust the input features of the 
multi-scale convolution. The module employs a multi-branch design with kernel sizes of 3, 5, and 7 for each 
branch, achieving a global receptive field equivalent to large-scale convolution kernels by stacking two depthwise 
strip convolutions. The choice of depthwise strip convolution is primarily based on two considerations: first, it 
significantly reduces computational load through a decomposed structure (for instance, replacing the standard 
7 × 7 convolution with a combination of 7 × 1 and 1 × 7 convolutions); second, for strip-shaped objects commonly 
found in segmentation scenarios (such as human bodies and utility poles), strip convolution complements 
traditional grid convolution, effectively enhancing the extraction capability of slender spatial features. The input 
data of the module undergoes depthwise convolution and subsequently generates multi-scale feature maps 
through parallel three-branch strip-shaped convolutions.

DLKCM
The previous module successfully achieved feature fusion and enhancement. To further improve the model’s 
global perception capabilities, this study proposes a deformable large-kernel convolutional module that integrates 
a bionic visual perception mechanism, as illustrated in Fig. 4. This module emulates the global perception 
capability of the self-attention mechanism through large-sized convolutional kernels, effectively circumventing 
the high computational costs associated with traditional self-attention modules while preserving the advantages 
of wide-area modeling. The introduction of deformable convolution allows for dynamic optimization of 
sampling positions, enhancing the model’s feature adaptability to diverse data distributions through its adaptive 
deformation capabilities. This significantly improves detection capabilities for small and irregularly shaped 
targets, particularly under complex backgrounds or varying lighting conditions. The proposed deformable large-
kernel convolution module employs a wide-range modeling mechanism, constructing a parameter-efficient ultra-
large receptive field through a composite structure of depthwise separable convolution and dilated convolution. 
This design substantially reduces computational load while simulating the global perception characteristics of 
the self-attention mechanism via a hierarchical convolution kernel decomposition strategy. According to the 
schematic diagram of the deformable convolution architecture, its core operational process can be divided into 
two key stages: First, the 3 × 3 deformable convolution layer module extracts initial features and generates a 
dynamic offset field, referred to as the Offsets module, which is vividly likened to a grid with arrows representing 
the adaptive spatial position offsets of each sampling point on the feature map.

Experiment
Experimental setup
As shown in Table 1, this study utilizes a hardware platform comprising an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 GPU 
and an Intel Xeon Silver 4214R CPU (2.40 GHz), with the models operating in a Python 3.9 environment. 
The training strategy employs a fixed learning rate of 0.0001 and a momentum parameter of 0.9, deliberately 
excluding early stopping mechanisms and data augmentation techniques. This configuration underscores the 
foundational and stable nature of the experimental design, as the omission of augmentation and early stopping 
mitigates confounding variables, while the low learning rate facilitates smooth convergence.
Dateset
The image examples of the dataset used in this study are shown in Fig. 5. The VisDrone2019 dataset is a widely 
utilized public resource that focuses on computer vision tasks from a drone’s perspective, including object 
detection, object tracking, and crowd counting. Released by the Machine Learning and Data Mining Lab at 
Tianjin University, the dataset was constructed by collecting data from various UAV models across diverse 
scenarios, including urban, suburban, and transportation hubs. This collection took into account complex

SIMD (Satellite Imagery for Multiscale Vehicle Detection) is a dataset designed for vehicle detection from 
drone and satellite perspectives, developed by a team from the National University of Sciences and Technology 
(NUST) in Pakistan. This dataset emphasizes multiscale vehicle object detection in complex scenarios, 
particularly addressing the challenge of recognizing small objects in low-altitude aerial images. It comprises 
15 categories and 5,000 high-resolution images, each with dimensions of 1024 × 768 pixels, along with detailed 
vehicle classifications (such as cars and trucks). SIMD is specifically crafted to address challenges associated with 
multiscale objects, low contrast, and dense arrangements in low-altitude imagery, thereby supporting intelligent 
urban traffic perception. The dataset offers comprehensive annotations, including occlusion status and scene 
visibility. In contrast, VisDrone focuses on multi-task generalization, while SIMD explores the algorithmic 
robustness of vehicle detection. Together, they provide a critical data foundation for environmental perception 
and target recognition research from the perspective of unmanned aerial vehicles.
To verify the robustness of our algorithm, we conducted validation on two additional datasets: RSOD and 
NWPU VHR-10. RSOD is an open-source benchmark dataset designed for remote sensing image object detection 
tasks, encompassing four typical types of ground objects: aircraft, oil tanks, playgrounds, and overpasses. The 
dataset aims to enhance semantic understanding and foster algorithmic innovation in high-resolution remote 
sensing scenarios, and it strictly adheres to the PASCAL VOC annotation standards. The data is organized into 
four independent subsets, each corresponding to image samples of different target types, such as aircraft clusters 
in airport areas and oil storage facilities in industrial zones. Each category is accompanied by meticulously 
annotated files, which facilitate few-shot learning and domain adaptation research.
The NWPU VHR-10 dataset is a high-resolution remote sensing image object detection dataset released by 
Northwestern Polytechnical University (NWPU) in China. It comprises over 800 visible and infrared remote 
sensing images, encompassing 10 typical target categories, such as aircraft, ships, oil tanks, and baseball fields. 
This dataset is particularly suitable for military reconnaissance and civilian resource monitoring. The annotations 
provided include bounding boxes and target category labels, with certain data featuring rotated bounding box 
annotations to address the challenges posed by varying orientations of aerial targets. The dataset’s characteristics 
comprise complex backgrounds, including airports and ports, significant variations in target scales—ranging 
from vehicles as small as tens of pixels to ships as large as hundreds of pixels—and multimodal information, 
where visible light and infrared data complement each other.
Training equipment and evaluation indicators
All experiments were conducted under a standardized hardware configuration to eliminate environmental 
variable interference, thus ensuring the reliability and reproducibility of the results. The study employed a 
phased validation process: initially, parameter optimization was performed based on the training set, followed 
by validation on an independent test set. In scenarios with limited sample sizes, a hold-out validation strategy 
was implemented. We will conduct experiments on the VisDrone2019 and SIMD datasets to validate the model’s 
effectiveness. Additionally, to demonstrate the model’s robustness, further validation will be performed using 
the RSOD and NWPU VHR-10 datasets. Given GPU limitations and training duration, the input size was set to

with a base learning rate configured at 1e-4 and a momentum coefficient set at 0.9. To comprehensively evaluate

Discussion and conclusion
This study addresses the core challenges of tiny object detection in remote sensing images—specifically, the 
small size of tiny objects, complex backgrounds, and limited computational resources—by proposing a 
dynamic feature enhancement detection framework, DFE-DETR, based on the improved RT-DETR. The model 
achieves a synergistic breakthrough in both accuracy and efficiency through a triple collaborative optimization 
mechanism: the dynamic sparse attention module (SAEM) reduces computational complexity, the multi-scale 
convolutional attention module (MSCAEM) enhances feature extraction for slender objects, and the deformable 
large kernel convolutional module (DLKCM) optimizes the localization of irregular objects. Experiments 
conducted on four datasets, including VisDrone2019 and SIMD, demonstrate that DFE-DETR achieves 
significant performance advantages with only 23.6 M parameters; it reaches 47.34% mAP@0.5 on VisDrone2019, 
surpassing many superior models, and 82.79% mAP@0.5 on SIMD, while maintaining real-time performance 
at 74.6 FPS. This validates its lightweight deployment value in embedded scenarios such as disaster response 
and traffic monitoring. However, there remains room for improvement in the model’s recall rate for extremely 
small targets, such as bicycles and covered tricycles. For instance, the mAP@0.5 for bicycle-like objects is only 
20.5%, and the recall rate of 16.5% for covered tricycles in VisDrone highlights the limitations of detection in 
densely occluded scenes. Employing highly targeted data augmentation techniques, such as physically realistic 
occlusion simulation, complex background synthesis, and weather disturbances, can significantly enhance 
the model’s robustness to local incomplete features. In terms of training strategies, it is essential to design an 
adaptive scale sampling mechanism that ensures the network fully learns multi-granularity representations of 
extremely small targets and partially occluded objects during the training process. This approach helps avoid 
insufficient learning of small targets, which often results from scale bias in conventional multi-scale training. At 
the model architecture level, it is crucial to strengthen the model’s discriminative ability under sparse occlusion. 
Introducing a local-global collaborative attention mechanism can effectively prioritize the focus on local key 
feature regions that are not occluded. Additionally, knowledge distillation—transferring occlusion robustness 
knowledge from high-precision large models to lightweight models—can mitigate missed detections effectively. 
In the future, the approach will rely on data augmentation, with parameter tuning and module combination 
conducted through quantitative evaluation feedback. This will systematically address core challenges related to 
insufficient representation capabilities for small objects, similar classes, and occluded objects in dense scenes.
